| **Containment** | Exercise bypasses, disable functions, guardbands, isolation mechanisms, and fallbacks against specific target faults or attacks. | Cannot claim implementation will contain or recover from failure. |
| **Operational readiness** | Confirm tool access, engineer veto rights and instrumentation to challenge anomalous tool returns, and recorded decision authority. | Cannot claim transferred workflow is operable, challengeable, or capable of supporting commitment. |
: **Target obligations define required measurements.** Untested boundaries remain explicit in the architectural record. {#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[25,45,30]"}

In @tbl-ch9-target-tests, the cheap-screen row separates executable reuse from predictive validity: a fast screen such as SCALE-Sim transfers as an empirical check, never as a verdict. Its validated coverage on the target (the share of comparisons it settles within declared error against a reference that can observe the property at risk) must be measured anew, and the screening economics that @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization works out apply only to that target-measured coverage.

The same test applies well beyond the array across learned, software, and physical artifacts (@tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests). A learned congestion predictor of the kind evaluated with CircuitNet [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet] carries its fitted relationships into a new process only after target requalification, just as ChiPBench evaluates placement algorithms on their final power, performance, and area rather than treating an intermediate proxy metric as the outcome [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench]. Similarly, a vendor's reported MLPerf software gain [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware] holds only for the version pair that produced it, while at the physical end of the range, the Cougar Point correction [@Intel2011CougarPoint] shows that any containment strategy transfers only as far as the failure mechanism it can actually reach.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learned congestion predictor trained on specific process, library, and design family** | Target process, standard-cell library, netlist family, placement flow, or routed-result definition shifts. | Requalify unchanged predictor; recalibrate, adapt, retrain, or retire only after isolating what fails. | Measure class-specific target errors and decision quality against held-out routed target results. |
| **H100 results across MLPerf Training v2.1/v3.0, with vendor software attribution** [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware] | Subsequent compiler, library, workload, or hardware generation alters configuration. | Constrain published improvement to reported versions/workloads; rerun comparison for new pair. | Repeat end-to-end workload measurement, pinning complete hardware and software configurations under identical result definitions. |
| **Cougar Point containment and correction results** [@Intel2011CougarPoint] | Target defect and remediation mechanisms differ. Intel required revised silicon and replacement programs. | For the reported SATA-degradation defect, distinguish temporary containment from the revised silicon needed for permanent correction. | Exercise corrected silicon and containment strategies against the target failure class before claiming correction. |
: **Transfer tests apply across learned, software, and physical components.** Actions follow changed dependencies, and target checks observe specific claimed failures or improvements. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests tbl-colwidths="[22,26,24,28]"}

Across all of these cases, reusing components never alters decision rights. Automated systems propose or screen candidates within declared studies, while named architects and reviewers remain responsible for freezes, waivers, signoffs, and tapeout decisions (@sec-what-architect-owns). The source study structure and reference candidate can support target exploration, while the original source conclusion remains attached to the conditions that established it.

## Open Questions {#sec-patterns-open-questions}

When we carry models, tools, and design records across workloads, compilers, process nodes, or packages, five open research questions remain:

- **When we reuse a fast screening model on a new target, how do we keep it from quietly ruling out the best candidate designs?** If a team checks a source-trained surrogate on a small target sample, that test catches weak designs that were wrongly promoted, yet it says nothing about viable architectures that the stale filter rejected before physical evaluation. When a workload shifts from dense matrix tiles to irregular sparse attention or a floorplan moves to a new metal stack, a conservative surrogate can discard the exact structural changes the target problem needs without raising an error flag. A team can spot-check a random subset of rejected candidates with a reference simulator or place-and-route flow to expose those missed opportunities, but every audit spends compute budget that could otherwise evaluate top-ranked proposals. We still lack practical ways to combine uncertainty estimates under distribution shift with adaptive auditing so that a team can bound how much performance gain the filter might be missing as the search distribution evolves.

- **How can we tell whether a hardware speedup will survive a change in compiler scheduling without running a full autotuner on every candidate?** When a team pins the compiler snapshot, a source-to-target comparison becomes reproducible, yet that freeze also locks in scheduling heuristics that may favor one candidate by accident. An accelerator can outperform its baseline simply because its scratchpad capacity and systolic dimensions divide evenly into a Triton or Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) loop-tiling pass, meaning the measured gain comes from a fragile match between one datapath and one lowering heuristic rather than a durable hardware improvement. An architect can expose those brittle wins by perturbing problem dimensions or retuning schedules for each candidate, but running a full compiler autotuner inside every hardware evaluation quickly exhausts the search budget. We still need low-cost sensitivity checks and representations that separate a datapath's underlying capability from a lucky compiler alignment before the hardware interface is frozen.

- **How can we separate what a learned timing or congestion model captures about circuit structure from the physics of a single process node?** Although the transfer map distinguishes a circuit representation from the numerical relationships fitted on top of it, most graph-based timing and congestion surrogates tangle netlist topology together with the cell delays, metal pitches, and pin-access rules of a single process design kit. When a design migrates from FinFETs to gate-all-around nanosheets or adopts a backside power delivery network, that coupling invalidates the model's wire-parasitic and routing predictions even when the register-transfer level structure is unchanged. Much as sim-to-real transfer in robotics separates rigid-body kinematics from surface-specific actuator calibration, a circuit representation that separates logic connectivity from node-specific physical calibration layers could sharply reduce how many routed target layouts a team must generate to requalify the predictor, provided the adapted surrogate still ranks worst-case slack and congestion accurately near the signoff boundary.

- **When a team modifies one block on a die, how can it tell which unedited neighbors still have valid timing and power evidence without rerunning full-chip signoff?** Selective requalification saves engineering time only when the dependency map catches every property a target change can disturb. Incremental timing analysis[^fn-incremental-sta-c09] updates arrival times along modified logic cones [@OpenROADDocs], yet repositioning an SRAM macro or resizing a tile buffer can also shift clock-tree insertion delay, capacitive crosstalk, and dynamic voltage drop across neighboring blocks that share no logical wires with the edited module. A dependency check that follows only structural netlist connectivity understates the affected slice, whereas rerunning full-chip extraction and electrothermal signoff after every local edit wipes out the time savings of modular transfer. We still lack fast physical-sensitivity bounds that can be paired with structural dependency graphs to tell an architect when an unedited neighbor's timing and power evidence remains valid.

[^fn-incremental-sta-c09]: **Incremental static timing analysis**: An optimization in physical design signoff where timing graphs are updated only for logic cones and net parasitics directly affected by an incremental circuit or placement modification, rather than recomputing the full chip. In a transfer setting, an incremental update understates the change if macro repositioning alters global clock-tree insertion delay or coupling on neighboring paths that the update treats as undisturbed.

- **How can we predict whether a block-level performance or power advantage will survive when a design is split across chiplets?** Chiplets joined by die-to-die links such as Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) promise modular hardware reuse, letting teams assemble pre-qualified compute dies and memory controllers into new product tiers without full-chip redesign. Even when each die's internal RTL and local timing closure carry forward intact, partitioning a shared coherence domain or systolic dataflow across package substrates introduces protocol-adapter latency, bump capacitance, and thermal coupling between stacked or adjacent dies. Single-die performance and power models miss those boundary penalties, while full multi-die cosimulation is too slow for early exploration. We still need interface-level abstractions and contracts that let an architect predict when a block-level advantage will hold up in a multi-die package before committing to substrate routing and thermal verification.

## Summary {#sec-patterns-summary}

The transfer test turns source-to-target differences into a concrete plan for either requalifying existing components or opening a new architectural study. An admission check first asks whether the decision itself survived the move; four stages then assign each unit an action and pair changed dependencies with checks able to observe the resulting risk. Even within the book's own executed record, transposing a matrix workload preserved the ranking of two systolic array shapes while changing their margin. In the prospective Lighthouse application (@sec-cross-stack-pattern-transfer), that gap widens across the stack: simulator outputs and candidate identities remain useful historical material, whereas workload coverage, the executable software path, memory costs, and implementation behavior all require fresh target evidence. Because the transfer map separates reusable components from source conclusions, exploration can reuse source work while leaving room to generate and evaluate different hardware and software organizations when the target requires them.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Components move, conclusions do not.** Data sources, models, tool paths, and checks remain reusable while their invariants and dependencies hold; a source conclusion remains applicable only where its supporting conditions still hold. Changed or uncertain dependencies require new evidence.
- **Check the decision before the components.** An admission check asks whether the question itself changed; unit actions and target checks follow only once that is settled, and a changed question reopens every claim tied to it.
- **Materiality is claim-specific.** A change reopens a claim when it alters the candidate identity, executable path, measured quantity, objective, decision rule, ranking, constraint verdict, or physical mechanism; magnitude alone decides nothing.
- **Transfer benefit needs a matched arm.** A carried prior earns its place only against a target-only arm with the same tasks, budgets, and stopping rules, with adaptation and requalification charged to the transfer.
- **A transferred result carries its compiler version.** Retain hardware and software snapshots with the inputs and procedures needed to repeat a comparison, and test software sensitivity before attributing a gain to microarchitecture, since a comparison that pins the hardware but not the toolchain can mistake compiler maturity for a hardware gain.
:::

Once we know which components and claims survive a move from one study to the next, the remaining step is to evaluate the complete approach across repeated, varied, and adversarial architectural studies (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). Where the source-to-target map identifies which claims each changed study must establish, controlled multi-study evaluation tests whether an AI-native design system improves the architecture result, reduces the total engineering cost of achieving it, or does both.
